Seen at %1$d separate places under %2$d rotating addresses, spread over %3$d m. Open AMBIT to review the evidence.
Passive RSSI visualization - not location. Distance is estimated from signal strength; bearing is arbitrary.
Wi-Fi circle | BLE square | ring spacing is estimated distance
Wi-Fi points: %1$d | BLE points: %2$d | Last refresh: %3$ss
Location permission not granted. Android returns no scan results at all without it.
Wi-Fi is switched off. Turn it on to observe; the app never connects to anything.
Waiting for the first scan to return.
Not scanning. Press START WI-FI to begin.
Scan throttling active. Android caps startScan at 4 calls per 2 minutes. Turn off "Wi-Fi scan throttling" in Developer Options for a faster refresh.
BLE is optional. Start it when you want Bluetooth observation.
This device reports no Bluetooth LE support.
Most BLE addresses rotate every ~15 minutes, so this count overstates how many physical devices are present.
Write a snapshot of the current environment to a file you can share yourself.
Built on-device. The debrief is plain text you can paste into any model you choose - the app never sends it anywhere itself.
WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT DO

Observes: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth metadata broadcast publicly by nearby hardware. Does not identify people or vehicles. Does not intercept traffic. Advertisement and beacon metadata only. Does not find a camera recording to an SD card. Only things actively broadcasting. Cannot give a bearing. One antenna gives distance estimates, not direction. No camera. No microphone. No network calls. No accounts.

Bluetooth trackers rotate their address every few minutes, so the address is useless as identity. Instead each advertisement is reduced to a signature: company ID, service UUIDs, payload shape, and the payload bytes that stay fixed across a key rotation. A signature is flagged only when it turns up at three or more spatially separated GPS fixes, with a real time gap between them, outside any place you have marked as known. The threshold is deliberately high. Two locations is usually a coincidence, and an alert that cries wolf gets ignored.

Nothing has met the threshold. This is the expected state. Correlation needs GPS fixes at several separate places over time, so a session that has not moved will never produce an alert no matter what is nearby.
This is a correlation, not an identification. Check whether it belongs to you or someone you were with before treating it as anything else.
That device is no longer in the log.
Not enough sightings yet to draw a trace.
RSSI over time, fixed -100 to -20 dBm scale. Movement here is as often multipath or body shadowing as it is real distance change.
No sighting of this device carried a GPS fix, so it cannot contribute to correlation.
Below 30s, Android will refuse most of these requests and serve cached results instead. Turn off "Wi-Fi scan throttling" in Developer Options to make it real.
Correlation is suppressed inside a known place. Without this, a tracker in your own home flags itself every day and you stop reading the alerts.
Everything runs on-device. No network calls, no telemetry, no accounts. Vendor names come from a bundled copy of the public IEEE OUI registry.

A passive observer of the radio environment around you. It logs Wi-Fi and Bluetooth broadcasts over time, names the manufacturer behind an address where it can, and warns you if a Bluetooth beacon appears to be following you between places. Everything happens on this device.

It cannot find a camera recording to an SD card. Only things actively broadcasting appear. It cannot identify people or vehicles. It does not intercept traffic - advertisement and beacon metadata only. It cannot tell you which direction something is in. One antenna gives a rough distance, never a bearing. Vendor labels describe a manufacturer, not who owns a device or what it is being used for.

Android ties every scan result to the location permission. Without it, the system returns an empty list and there is nothing to show at all. That is a platform rule, not a choice this app made. Location is also what makes the tracker correlator work: deciding whether a beacon has followed you means knowing you were in different places. Your position is written to the local log and nowhere else.
No network permission is requested. No telemetry, no accounts, no cloud. Exports are plain files that stay on your phone until you share them yourself.
No location fix yet. Wait for GPS and try again.
Correlation complete. Nothing met the threshold.
Machine-readable snapshots. Timestamps are UTC epoch milliseconds alongside ISO-8601, so a file still means something a year from now.
A plain-text summary of the environment: totals, density, band spread, category breakdown, notable hardware, and the limits of the method. Readable as-is, or pasted wherever you need it.
This shows signal strength, not direction or distance. Move slowly and watch whether the signal gets stronger or weaker.
Listening for this tracker. Walk around slowly.
Signal lost. Go back to where it was strongest.
Vibrate faster as the signal gets stronger
Beep faster as the signal gets stronger
Your body blocks Bluetooth. Turn in place slowly: the signal is usually strongest when you face the tracker. Readings settle over a second or two.
Ask the tracker to beep so you can hear where it is. Works only while the tracker is away from its owner.
This tracker\'s network doesn\'t let other people make it beep. Use the signal meter and the search tips instead.
The tracker has to be in range first.
Asked the tracker to beep. Listen for it.
Done. You can try again if you didn\'t hear it.

Ambit will connect to this tracker over Bluetooth and ask it to play its sound. This is the only time Ambit sends anything. Nothing goes over the internet.\n\nThe tracker only beeps while it is away from its owner. Its owner might be able to tell that someone connected to it.
This address is randomized and may change while you search. Locate from a tracker alert follows rotations; this view can\'t.
HOW TO FIND AND DISABLE IT
Bluetooth connect permission is needed. Grant it in the app\'s settings.
Couldn\'t connect. Move closer and try again.
This tracker doesn\'t offer a sound we can trigger.
The tracker refused. It may be near its owner right now.
No answer from the tracker. Move closer and try again.

If you think someone is tracking you on purpose, think about your safety first. Switching the tracker off may show the person who placed it that it was found.

Before you disable it, photograph it where you found it and note the date, time and place. Keep Ambit's alert. If you report it, the police may want the tracker itself; manufacturers can sometimes identify the owner when the police ask.

Local support services for stalking or domestic abuse can help you plan what to do next.
Typical shape only. Designs change between models.
AirTag: a white disc about 3 cm across, slightly domed, with a polished metal back. Other Find My accessories come as cards, key fobs and bike mounts, and look like ordinary products.

AirTag: press down on the polished metal back and turn it anticlockwise until it stops.\nLift off the cover and remove the round coin-cell battery.\nOther Find My accessories: look for a battery door or a slot that takes a coin. Sealed cards can\'t be switched off; keep them away from you or hand them to the police.
A small rounded square, about 4 cm wide, with a hole in one corner for a key ring. Usually black, white or a pastel colour.
Original SmartTag and SmartTag+: prise the case apart at the small notch on the edge.\nSmartTag2: open the battery cover on the back.\nRemove the coin-cell battery.
Made by several companies (for example Chipolo, Pebblebee, Motorola and eufy). Shapes include discs, rounded squares, key fobs and wallet-sized cards.

Look for a twist-off or slide-off back hiding a coin-cell battery.\nCard-shaped and rechargeable models are often sealed and can\'t be opened.\nIf your phone has unknown tracker alerts in its safety settings, it may show the maker\'s own instructions.
Usually a rounded square with a hole for a key ring (Mate, Pro), a thin card (Slim) or a small adhesive disc (Sticker).

Mate and Pro: open the case at the seam to reach the battery. Some newer models twist open.\nSlim and Sticker are sealed and can\'t be switched off. Keep them away from you or hand them to the police.
Round or rounded-square tags with a hole for a key ring, or a thin card. Often brightly coloured.
Round models: twist the cover to reach the coin-cell battery.\nCard models are sealed and can\'t be switched off.
Ambit couldn\'t match this signal to a known tracker network. It may be a tracker, a fitness band, a beacon or something else that broadcasts over Bluetooth.
Use the signal meter to find where it is strongest.\nLook for anything small you don\'t recognise.\nIf you find a device, look for a battery door or a power button.

Bags: inner pockets, the lining, under the base panel, wallets.
Coats: pockets and hoods, sometimes sewn into the lining.
Cars: under seats, between seat cushions, in the glovebox, door pockets, the boot or trunk lining, under the spare wheel.
Outside the car: wheel wells, behind bumpers, under the chassis, often in a magnetic case.
Bikes and scooters: under the saddle, inside the frame tube, in lights or bells.
Gifts and shared items: toys, phone cases, keyrings, children's belongings.

Start Locate mode and walk slowly around the area where the alert happened.
When the signal is HOT, stop and check everything within about an arm's length.
Check one item at a time: move a bag or coat away, then see if the signal follows it.
If the tracker supports it, use Play sound and listen.
No signal does not prove there is no tracker. Some only broadcast now and then.
A tracker that follows the IETF DULT standard for detecting unwanted trackers. Any brand can support it, so it may be a disc, a square tag, a card or something built into another product.

Use Play sound to hear where it is.\nLook for a battery door, a twist-off back or a slot that takes a coin.\nSealed or rechargeable trackers may not switch off. Keep them away from you or hand them to the police.
Small rounded tags and key fobs, and wallet-sized cards. Many are rechargeable.
Use Play sound to hear where it is.\nRechargeable models have no battery to remove. Some can be switched off with a long press on the button; otherwise keep it away from you or hand it to the police.

A Wi-Fi network that appeared at several places you went. Most often it is a phone hotspot of someone travelling the same way, or the Wi-Fi of a bus, train or car. It could also be a portable camera or a tracker with Wi-Fi.

Check whether the network name belongs to a vehicle you used or a person you travelled with.\nIf you can\'t explain it, search your car and bags as you would for a Bluetooth tracker.\nWi-Fi trackers usually have a power button or a battery pack.
Possible camera glasses (Meta or Luxottica Bluetooth). Could also be a VR headset or other Meta hardware.
Named like a camera in setup mode. It may be a camera someone is setting up nearby.
Named like a smart-home gadget in setup mode.
Made by a company that mainly sells cameras. Its network or hotspot may belong to a camera.
Waits for 4 places spread over a wider area and at least 45 minutes. Fewest false alarms; slowest to warn.
3 places at least 250 m apart over 20 minutes or more. A balance between speed and false alarms.
3 places at least 150 m apart over 10 minutes or more. Warns sooner on short trips, but more likely to flag someone who simply travels the same way.
Alert on Wi-Fi networks that travel with me
Usually a phone hotspot or the Wi-Fi of a bus, train or car. Needs Wi-Fi scanning on.
Alert when camera glasses may be nearby
Matches Meta and Luxottica Bluetooth IDs at close range. VR headsets and controllers use the same IDs. At most one alert every 15 minutes.
A close-range Bluetooth device uses Meta or Luxottica IDs, as Ray-Ban Meta and similar glasses do. It could also be a VR headset or other Meta hardware.
Seen at %1$d separate places, spread over %2$d m. Often a hotspot on a nearby phone, or a bus, train or car network. Open Ambit to review.

This network was seen at several places you went. It may be a hotspot on someone\'s phone nearby, or the Wi-Fi of a bus, train or car you rode in. Locate isn\'t available for Wi-Fi, because Android allows only a few Wi-Fi scans every two minutes.
A weighting of the evidence, not a probability.
Moved with you from one place to the next %1$d times
Said it is away from its owner
Strong signal at %1$d places, so it was close to you, not just nearby
Belongs to a known tracker network
Not a known tracker type, so this is less certain
Wi-Fi networks often travel with other people, so this is less certain
Nothing trusted yet. Use \"This is mine\" on an alert for your own tags.
Your %1$d paired Bluetooth devices (headphones, watch, car) are never flagged.
Apple and Google tags change their identity about once a day, so trusting one of them only lasts about a day.
Maps never download anything. The built-in map shows coastlines, lakes and borders. For streets, import a raster MBTiles file you made or downloaded yourself.
That file isn\'t a raster MBTiles map. Vector tiles aren\'t supported.
The sightings behind this alert are no longer stored. They may have been removed by the data retention setting.
Numbers are the places in the order they were visited. Positions come from the phone\'s location fix and can be off by tens of metres.
REPORT FOR POLICE OR A SUPPORT WORKER
A PDF with the timeline, every sighting, a map, and an explanation of how the data was collected and what it cannot prove. It stays on your phone until you choose where to send it.
Confidence score (app\'s weighting of the evidence, not a probability)
Local time UTC Latitude Longitude ±m dBm Bluetooth address

The phone listened for Bluetooth Low Energy advertisements, the short public broadcasts that trackers send so their owner\'s network can find them. It did not connect to, decode the contents of, or interfere with the tracker. Each time the tracker was heard, the phone stored the time, the received signal strength and the phone\'s own GPS position. Trackers change their Bluetooth address regularly; the app grouped sightings using the identifier each tracker network keeps stable while the tracker is away from its owner. An alert is raised only when the same tracker is heard at three or more places at least 250 m apart and moved between them with the phone.

It cannot identify the tracker\'s owner or who placed it. It cannot show where the tracker is now, or exactly how close it was: signal strength gives only a rough idea of distance. Positions are the phone\'s, not the tracker\'s, and can be off by tens of metres. A tracker carried by someone travelling the same way would produce a similar pattern. Tracker networks change their advertising formats, so the tracker type is the app\'s best match, not a certainty.

SHA-256 of the sightings table in canonical form: %1$s. Recomputing it from the same data gives the same value, which shows the table was not edited after this report was made. It does not prove anything about the data before that.
4 to 12 digits. If you forget it, you\'ll have to clear the app\'s data and lose its history.
Lock the app with a PIN
Asks for the PIN every time the app is opened. Tracking keeps running in the background.
Hide the app in recent apps
Also blocks screenshots of the app. Turn it off when you want to screenshot evidence.
Changes the home-screen icon and name. The real name still shows in the phone\'s app list, settings and notification headers.
Quick exit goes straight to the home screen and removes the app from recent apps.
Alerts say only \"Reminder\" and are hidden on the lock screen.
Open the app when you have a moment.
IF YOU ARE IN DANGER NOW
Call your local emergency number. If it isn\'t safe to talk, many emergency services accept text messages or silent calls; check how yours works when you can.

Services for people experiencing stalking or domestic abuse can help you understand your options and make a safety plan.\nMany run free, confidential helplines and chat services. Search for one in your country from a device the other person can\'t check.\nA doctor, a trusted friend, or a workplace or school welfare officer can also help you find support.

Export the PDF report from the alert's evidence screen and keep a copy somewhere the other person can't reach.
Photograph any tracker you find where you found it, before you touch it.
Write down dates, times and places of anything that worried you.
The police may want the tracker itself. Manufacturers can sometimes identify the owner when the police ask.

Check location sharing in your maps, family and "find my device" apps.
Look for apps you don't recognise, especially ones with location or device admin access.
Change passwords for your main accounts from a safe device, and turn on two-step sign-in.
Check which devices are signed in to your accounts and remove ones you don't recognise.
Check your car's connected-car app, if it has one.

Removing a tracker or switching it off can show the person who placed it that it was found. Think about how they might react.\nA support service can help you decide when and how to act safely.\nYou don\'t have to do anything straight away. Ambit keeps recording in the background.
WHAT AMBIT CAN AND CAN\'T DO

Ambit can notice Bluetooth trackers and Wi-Fi networks that keep turning up wherever you go.\nIt can\'t find trackers that are switched off, GPS trackers that use only the mobile network, or spyware on your phone.\nNo alert does not mean no tracker. Trust your own judgement too.
Needed so scanning can keep recording positions after a restart. Choose \"Allow all the time\" on the next screen.
Not enough data yet. Check back after a few hours of scanning off the charger.

Ambit aims to use under 3% of the battery a day on Standard. Android doesn\'t let an app measure its own share, so this figure is the whole phone\'s use while Ambit was scanning; your phone\'s Battery settings show Ambit\'s share.
Your phone stopped Ambit in the background. Tap to start it again, then see Settings › Reliability to stop it happening.

Samsung: Settings › Apps › Ambit › Battery › Unrestricted. Then Settings › Battery › Background usage limits: make sure Ambit is not in Sleeping or Deep sleeping apps, and add it to Never sleeping apps.
Xiaomi, Redmi and POCO: Settings › Apps › Manage apps › Ambit. Turn on Autostart and set Battery saver to No restrictions. In recent apps, lock Ambit\'s card.
OnePlus, OPPO and realme: Settings › Apps › Ambit › Battery. Allow background activity and set it to not optimise. Lock Ambit in recent apps.
Huawei and Honor: Settings › Battery › App launch. Set Ambit to Manage manually and turn on Auto-launch, Secondary launch and Run in background.
vivo and iQOO: Settings › Battery › Background power consumption management. Allow high background power use for Ambit, and allow Autostart.
Motorola: Settings › Apps › Ambit › App battery usage › Unrestricted.
Pixel: Settings › Apps › Ambit › App battery usage › Unrestricted.

Set Ambit\'s battery use to Unrestricted or Don\'t optimise in the app\'s settings. Some phones also have an Autostart or App launch setting that must allow Ambit. The site dontkillmyapp.com lists steps for most brands.

For trips: alerts switch to High sensitivity, and you can mark a hotel or a friend\'s place as known just for the trip. On planes, trains and buses other passengers\' trackers travel with you too, so expect more alerts on those legs.

Shows whether scanning is on and how many alerts are open.
A live log of the raw Bluetooth advertisements Ambit receives: manufacturer data, service UUIDs and service data, with what Ambit made of each one.
Start Bluetooth scanning to see packets.
